ai.sum: Hudson Institute report challenges claims by I-MAK about drug patent evergreening in US pharmaceutical policy.

brief.summary: The authors, writing for Hudson Institute, argue that the Initiative for Medicines, Access, and Knowledge (I-MAK) drives congressional drug-patent policy with patent counts and exclusivity claims that do not survive scrutiny. They say I-MAK counts all patents and applications 'related to' a drug, including abandoned or irrelevant ones, and stacks their terms as 'evergreening'. The USPTO's 2024 study reached similar conclusions. The authors test I-MAK's claims on GLP-1 drugs and biologics, finding errors such as Lyrica and Rituxan, where generics or biosimilars entered years before I-MAK's claimed exclusivity ended. They conclude that the real evergreening is I-MAK's recurring brochures and its new Drug Patent Book, which keep feeding Washington with inaccurate claims, and that its numbers should not guide legislation.
brief.argument: I-MAK's patent counts and claimed exclusivity periods for drugs and biologics are methodologically unreliable and inaccurate, and they are being used to justify drug-patent legislation.
recommendations: Require I-MAK to disclose the specific patents and statistical methods behind its aggregate counts.
Base drug-patent policy on rigorous, replicable assessments rather than raw patent counts.
Rely on the USPTO and FDA's independent review rather than advocacy brochures.

ai.sum: CFR podcast discusses the US economic fallout from the midterm elections and cost-of-living pressures voters prioritise.

brief.summary: The authors, host Rebecca Patterson and KPMG chief economist Diane Swonk, read the midterm results as voter frustration with inflation, health-care costs and stagnant wages, and see a mandate for Congress to focus on cost of living and affordability. They point to household debt strain, with about 20 percent of households behind on debt payments, and blame data center construction for pushing up electricity and water costs and wages in skilled trades. On the labour market they describe a 'low hire, low fire' economy with low turnover, and they note that real wages have lagged inflation for 13 straight months. They argue inflation is concentrated in food, energy and health care and that shocks have become endemic rather than episodic. Swonk argues the Fed should be more decisive, forecasting at least two rate hikes by early next year, and rejects the view that inflation near 3 percent is acceptable.
brief.argument: The authors argue that voters have signalled that cost-of-living pressures are their top priority and that the Fed should tighten decisively because inflation shocks have become persistent.
recommendations: Congress should focus on cost of living and affordability.
The Fed should raise rates, with at least two hikes by early next year.
Financial literacy should be expanded because it narrows the opportunity gap and strengthens the economy.

7241a8128fe75872.title: Why this US midterm was unusually important for the Middle East

brief.summary: The authors argue that the midterm result was unusually consequential for the Middle East because Trump's Iran war and Israel policy drove both Democratic turnout and Republican disillusionment. They read Trump's announcement ending about four billion dollars in annual aid to Israel as evidence that US support for Israel is now a political liability on both right and left, and suggest it could pressure Netanyahu's opponents, with Gadi Eisenkot as likely next government former. They warn that Trump, having already reviewed Iran war plans and moved forces forward, could still escalate to avoid appearing a loser, though Iranian statements have so far been de-escalatory. They note that a Democratic Congress can block domestic legislation but has little power to restrain a president as commander in chief. A diplomatic deal resembling Vance's earlier memorandum would, in their view, only confirm the war as a disaster.
brief.argument: The midterm result, driven by the Iran war and Israel policy, makes Trump's Middle East choices a central political problem that could either calm or provoke an escalation with Iran.

989820f0181693b4.title: What the midterms will (and won’t) change for US foreign policy
989820f0181693b4.summary: Our experts explain where the power shift could change foreign policy—and where it won’t. The post What the midterms will (and won’t) change for US foreign policy appeared first on Atlantic Council .

ai.sum: Atlantic Council experts assess where the US midterm power shift could and could not change US foreign policy.

brief.summary: The authors argue that Democrats' sweep of both chambers of Congress gives them new leverage over spending and oversight, but that President Trump keeps substantial foreign-policy power, so the shift will matter in some areas and not others. Landon Derentz expects continued economic pressure on Iran and a possible military escalation, while Jonathan Panikoff sees a short window for strikes during the lame-duck period and a long, low-intensity conflict in the Middle East. Josh Lipsky expects spending deals that raise deficits, tariffs to persist despite voter anger, and possible bipartisan pushback on Canada tariffs and China trade. Torrey Taussig expects Democrats to shape allied policy through committee hearings, starting with the 2027 defense authorization and US troop levels in Europe. Jonathan expects US aid to Israel to change, though joint weapons production may continue. Landon argues Trump will rely more on executive authority, and that energy expansion could prove durable.
brief.argument: The midterm shift gives Congress new leverage over spending and oversight, but Trump's executive foreign-policy power will limit how much it changes US policy.

2db859ece5ee6817.title: The Rising Threat of Great Power War and the Lessons of 1914

ai.sum: A CFR essay analyzes the rising threat of great power war by drawing lessons from 1914.

brief.summary: The authors argue that the post-Cold War optimism that great power war had been overcome has collapsed, as rivalry, nationalism and autocratic cohesion return. Drawing on a conversation with historian Odd Arne Westad, they compare today's dispersing, multipolar order to the years before 1914, when economic and political power shifted and nationalism rose. They stress that wars can begin without leaders choosing them, as escalation logic overrides prudent planning. Their central lesson is that policymakers must understand past mistakes and end small conflicts before they grow into something far larger. They also note that information moves faster and artificial intelligence increasingly places some decisions beyond human control, making the lesson more urgent. The piece is presented as an interview-based essay rather than a set of formal policy prescriptions.
brief.argument: Great power war is a rising risk because today's multipolar, nationalist world resembles the pre-1914 system, and leaders can be pushed into escalation they do not want, so small conflicts must be ended early.

2b313abb30585f61.title: Europe’s Defence Coalitions Need Someone to Own the Outcome
2b313abb30585f61.summary: EU leaders are pushing capability coalitions. The next question is who is responsible when the capability does not materialise.

ai.sum: Analysis argues that EU defence capability coalitions need a clearly accountable owner when promised capabilities fail to materialise.

brief.summary: The author argues that EU capability coalitions are the right direction but face an accountability gap: European defence capacity is fragmented across national ministries, ports, railways, power grids, telecoms and private firms, and no institution owns the complete system. Rather than waiting for a single federal structure, he proposes starting with a few willing countries and a limited set of capabilities such as military mobility, logistics, air and missile defence, and surveillance. For each capability, a lead integrator (not a super-owner) would map the delivery chain, expose dependencies, monitor readiness and answer for whether the outcome can be produced. He suggests a 'Defence Capacity Statement' as a common discipline: required effect, usable capacity, critical dependencies, accountable owners and evidence. The Nordic and Baltic states are offered as a natural test case. The core message is outcome first, then visibility, control and accountability, with finance following capacity requirements.
brief.argument: Europe's fragmented defence capacity needs a designated lead integrator accountable for whether each agreed capability actually delivers its required outcome, rather than more coordination or a single common owner.
recommendations: Start with a small group of willing countries and a limited number of capabilities such as military mobility, logistics, air and missile defence, surveillance and energy resilience.
Designate a lead integrator for each agreed capability, responsible for the full delivery chain, unresolved dependencies, readiness and reporting on outcomes rather than ownership of assets.
Adopt a Defence Capacity Statement defining required effect, existing usable capacity, critical dependencies, accountable owners and evidence of delivery.
Map capabilities from the required outcome backwards, bringing civilian infrastructure owners such as ports, rail and grid operators into defence planning while keeping their ownership unchanged.

444ac683e844a78c.title: The Golden Dome Proposal is Destabilizing and Dangerous
444ac683e844a78c.summary: Editor’s Note: This is the second article in a two-part series exploring the Golden Dome for America proposal. Please also read the first, “Golden Dome Is Technologically and Financially Infeasible.”Golden Dome is an ambitious proposal for a comprehensive, layered defense, with ground, sea, and space-based elements. It is supposed to protect the United States, its allies, and deployed forces from attacks by ballistic missiles, cruise missiles, hypersonic boost-glide…

ai.sum: War on the Rocks publishes an article arguing the Golden Dome missile defence proposal is destabilizing and dangerous.

brief.summary: The authors, two physicists who led American Physical Society studies on missile defence, argue that the Golden Dome proposal would make the United States less safe even if it were never fully built. They say a budget in the hundreds of billions and an ambitious mandate would prompt adversaries to add warheads, develop evasive delivery systems, and build anti-satellite weapons to counter it. They add that boost-phase interception would compress crisis decision times to tens of seconds, pushing toward automated launch decisions. They also link the mandate's 'left of launch' attacks and the lapse of New START to rising nuclear risk. Their conclusion is that arms control agreements remain the only approach that has historically reduced the nuclear threat.
brief.argument: Golden Dome cannot provide effective protection against long-range ballistic missiles, and pursuing it would increase nuclear risk by provoking adversary buildups, countermeasures and faster, more mistake-prone crises.
recommendations: Recognise that any deployed strategic missile defence has only limited capability against even a small number of missiles, to avoid hair-trigger postures.
Treat arms control agreements as the only historically successful route to reducing the nuclear threat.
Avoid deploying boost-phase intercept systems that would require pre-delegated launch authority and automated threat assessment.

09fca973c74718c1.title: Who Repairs the Internet in Wartime?
09fca973c74718c1.summary: In spring 2026, Britain, Norway, and the United States tracked and disrupted a covert Arctic exercise off the coast of Norway involving Russian deep-sea submersibles simulating the deployment of a weapon designed to disable the two 1,400-kilometer submarine cables linking the islands of Svalbard to mainland Norway. Svalbard hosts a satellite ground station serving Europe, the United States, and Japan. This encounter revealed that NATO allies can detect a covert subsea…

ai.sum: Britain, Norway and the US disrupted a covert Russian deep-sea submersible exercise near Norway simulating attacks on Svalbard's subsea cables.

brief.summary: The authors argue that subsea cables are a wartime vulnerability the United States has not planned for. Routine faults are handled by about 22 specialised repair ships, but several simultaneous cuts across theatres would exhaust spare capacity and the repair queue, a scenario they say adversaries are rehearsing. They point to the Svalbard interception, China's cable-cutting device, and Russia's deep-sea submarines, and note that repair ships could become military targets, that war-risk insurance can be cancelled at short notice, and that Chinese-linked repair capacity cannot be assumed in a Taiwan crisis. They say the US has retired its government cable ship and funds only two contracted ships. They argue wartime repair should be treated as a national-security mission, with a federal coordinator, a larger funded fleet, trusted spares stockpiles, and tiered escort rules for contested waters.
brief.argument: The United States needs a wartime submarine cable repair and restoration strategy, because its current commercial repair system cannot handle simultaneous cuts across multiple theatres.
recommendations: Designate submarine cables a critical infrastructure subsector and create a federal restoration coordinator with emergency authority.
Expand and multiyear-fund the Cable Security Fleet, procure a government-owned repair ship, and stockpile trusted spare parts at US and allied ports.
Create pre-arranged government-backed war-risk insurance for repair ships before a crisis.
Adopt a graduated protection framework: close escort for government-contracted ships and area security for commercial ones, and negotiate allied arrangements in advance.
brief.turkey: Türkiye sits on Black Sea, Eastern Mediterranean and Red Sea-adjacent cable routes near the Russian and Middle Eastern theatres the piece describes, so the same repair-capacity and contested-waters risks bear on its own connectivity planning.

brief.summary: The authors argue that the Democratic sweep of the US midterms has sharpened Donald Trump's predicament over the war with Iran. Trump concedes the war cost his party votes but insists his Iran policy is right, and he is unwilling to let Congress scrutinise the conflict or its economic costs. Democrats, now holding congressional power, will press for an end to the war but have limited means to constrain a president with wide latitude abroad. The piece suggests Trump is pushed toward a quick conclusion, with his calculations resting on a Qatari-brokered channel and a readiness to use force if talks fail. It doubts Iranian offers are sincere, citing contradictory Iranian statements and Tehran's seven conditions. It also warns that last April's memorandum of understanding was short-lived and produced nothing.
brief.argument: Democratic control of Congress will pressure Trump to end the Iran war, but he is likely to push for a quick settlement via Qatar or force rather than change course.

brief.summary: The piece is a news roundup of German political reactions to the 2026 US midterm results, in which Democrats won majorities in both chambers of Congress. It gathers statements from parties across the spectrum: CDU's Jürgen Hardt reads the result as a verdict on Trump's foreign policy and notes the contradiction between Trump's stated aversion to military conflict and his actual use of force, including in Iran. SPD and Green figures stress that Trump remains unpredictable, so Europe must strengthen its own security. Defence minister Pistorius and NATO's Whitaker stress the stability of military ties and the continued validity of Article 5. The AfD sees Trump as still the decisive authority on foreign policy, and the Left links the vote to cost-of-living grievances. The article presents these as German reactions rather than an analytical verdict.
brief.argument: German political reactions to the Democratic midterm win are divided, with most expecting Trump to remain unpredictable in foreign policy, even as military cooperation with the US stays stable.
recommendations: Strengthen European security policy and defence capacity independently of the US
Maintain a pragmatic working relationship with the US administration regardless of party
Address domestic social and cost-of-living problems to counter right-wing authoritarianism

The main limit abroad is Congress: Democrats could block any easing of Russia sanctions, which they doubt Moscow is serious about. The Kremlin, they note, is trying to exploit Trump's weakened position to push for a Ukraine settlement favourable to Moscow. brief.argument: Trump's domestic weakness after the midterms will push him to concentrate on foreign policy, where he retains broad freedom of action, while Congress remains the main check on his Russia policy.

brief.summary: The authors examine whether the Yemeni army can break into Houthi-held Al-Jawf governorate, with the aim of eventually reaching Sana'a. They argue that recapturing mountains such as Huwashiyan and pushing toward al-Hazm would strengthen government depth in Marib, ease Saudi border threats, and force the Houthis to divert forces to defend Sa'ada. They stress that Al-Jawf's tribal networks give mobilisation capacity and that Houthi repression has bred local resentment, so credible military gains could widen an anti-Houthi coalition. The authors caution, however, that success depends on sustaining the offensive, keeping the army unified, and overcoming fortifications, and that stabilisation and good governance must follow quickly. They also note that tribal opposition to the Houthis does not automatically mean support for the government, since tribal leaders will resist both if excluded from power and wealth.
brief.argument: A Yemeni army push into Al-Jawf could reverse Houthi territorial control, but only if it is sustained, unified and paired with tribal incorporation and rapid stabilisation.
recommendations: Prioritise stabilisation, state-building and good governance immediately after any military gains
Establish a unified chain of command for the offensive
Support local development to rebuild trust between communities and the state
Incorporate tribal leaders and give them a share of wealth and power to avoid renewed opposition

brief.summary: The authors argue that Washington's embrace of Morocco's autonomy-under-sovereignty plan for Western Sahara undermines the UN-led peace process and worsens regional tensions. They trace how the 2020 reversal of longstanding US policy, tied to the Abraham Accords, shifted the diplomatic landscape, and note that US backing has been expressed through economic projects, consular moves and efforts to sideline the Polisario. They say this has fuelled Algerian anxiety, prompting Algiers to re-engage in the Sahel, normalise ties with Mali, and cut relations with the UAE. The piece concludes that by choosing a side, Washington may have made regional peace less likely, even as it claims to want to end the frozen conflict.
brief.argument: US backing of Morocco's Western Sahara plan is incompatible with its stated goal of brokering peace and is deepening zero-sum rivalry in North Africa and the Sahel.

fb0a9cb2f2a16859.title: Washington should broaden its Shia outreach in Iraq. Muqtada al-Sadr is a case study.
fb0a9cb2f2a16859.summary: Conversations with several Sadrists reveal a movement preparing to fill a leadership vacuum in Iraq—and engage with the US. The post Washington should broaden its Shia outreach in Iraq. Muqtada al-Sadr is a case study. appeared first on Atlantic Council .

ai.sum: An Atlantic Council analysis argues Washington should broaden its outreach to Iraqi Shia actors, using Muqtada al-Sadr's movement as a case study.

brief.summary: The authors read Muqtada al-Sadr's October 2026 post addressed to Washington as a signal that he is repositioning as a nationalist, more open-to-the-US Shia alternative to the Coordination Framework. Drawing on conversations with Sadrists, they describe the movement preparing to return to power as the Framework's rule weakens under economic strain, with Iraq's oil revenue losses after the Hormuz closure and the stalled militia disarmament plan adding pressure. They identify two obstacles to his rise: eroded cohesion inside the Sadrist movement after years of withdrawal, and opposition from the Najaf clerical establishment that prefers multiple Shia factions in power. They conclude that Washington should stop treating Iraq's Shia as a reflection of Iran and widen its engagement with non-Iran-aligned Shia voices, with Gulf allies encouraged to do the same.
brief.argument: Al-Sadr is positioning himself as a viable, US-friendly Shia alternative to Iran-aligned ruling parties, and Washington should broaden its engagement with non-Iranian Shia voices in Iraq.
recommendations: Broaden engagement with the range of Shia voices in Iraq rather than treating the community as an extension of the Iranian regime

brief.summary: The author argues that Asian governments, though publicly silent after the US midterms, privately welcome Democratic control of Congress. They hope it will make Trump's Iran war decisions more predictable and push toward winding the war down, which has disrupted Asian energy markets. The author expects Congress to press for tougher China policy, support Taiwan arms sales, and curb tariffs, which Asian officials see as unpopular with Americans. However, the author warns that a lame-duck Trump, isolated from advisers, could be unpredictable and might resume attacks on Iran, which would hurt US standing in Asia. The piece treats the expected policy shifts as plausible but not assured.
brief.argument: Asian allies hope the post-midterm Congress will push US foreign policy, especially on Iran, but these hopes cannot be taken for granted given Trump's unpredictability.

852b8c5a4003f540.title: COP31 in Turkey: What to Expect
852b8c5a4003f540.summary: The 2026 UN climate summit faces mounting pressure to accelerate climate action and deliver on implementation, as projections indicate that the world will overshoot the 1.5°C (2.7°F) global warming threshold, raising questions about the legacy of the Paris Agreement.

ai.sum: Türkiye will host COP31 in 2026, with the summit facing pressure to accelerate climate action as the 1.5°C threshold looks likely to be overshot.

brief.summary: The authors preview COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye (9–20 November), which falls on the tenth anniversary of the Paris Agreement's entry into force and proceeds without an official US delegation. They argue that the summit's new COP31 presidency is pushing from pledges toward implementation, with an Action Agenda and voluntary pledges on electrification and sustainable AI. They note real progress, with projected warming down to about 2.8°C under current policies, but judge the 1.5°C goal out of reach. They identify finance, fossil fuel language, emissions reductions, adaptation metrics and a just transition mechanism as the main contested issues. They also flag headwinds such as delays in IPCC reporting and shifting national politics. Their conclusion is that COP31 will likely produce no single breakthrough, though its value lies in keeping climate on the global agenda and building coalitions, notably on methane.
brief.argument: COP31 is unlikely to yield a major breakthrough, and its value lies mainly in sustaining implementation pressure and coalition-building on climate action.
recommendations: Developed countries should deliver on existing climate finance commitments, including the goal of $300 billion per year by 2035.
Countries should accelerate methane emissions cuts, particularly in the oil and gas sectors, where low-cost options exist.
Parties should resolve the timeline for the next IPCC reports so that national commitments rest on current science.
brief.turkey: Türkiye hosts COP31 as president, and the authors' framing of implementation as the test of the summit places Ankara's presidency under scrutiny for delivering concrete outcomes.

(Getty Images) Toggle Table of Contents…

ai.sum: Hudson Institute analysts Tsiporah Fried and Luke Coffey argue the 2026 US midterm results are more complex than a simple Democratic wave.

brief.summary: The authors, two Hudson Institute analysts, argue that the November 2026 midterms were a vote of censure against Donald Trump rather than an endorsement of a Democratic platform. Voters judged his record against his promises, with cost of living as the leading concern, followed by anger over the Iran war, the handling of immigration enforcement, and perceived corruption. They describe the result as a real Democratic gain, including flips in conservative states, but caution that the Democratic coalition is held together more by opposition to Trump than by a shared agenda, and that its factions (progressive, pragmatic moderate, establishment) remain divided. On the Republican side they map competing currents (isolationists, prioritizers, Reaganites, nationalists) and argue the party brand has been punished, with succession to 2028 wide open. They read J.D. Vance's distancing from the president as constrained by his position, and see Marco Rubio's next moves as a test of how much he separates from the MAGA agenda. They close by urging France to abandon ideological readings of American politics.
brief.argument: The midterms were a rebuke of Trump's broken promises rather than a shift to a coherent Democratic ideology, and the post-Trump succession on both sides remains unsettled.

ai.sum: Atlantic Council analysis says recent Russian setbacks in the Balkans show Moscow struggling to retain influence as the Ukraine war nears its fifth year.

brief.summary: The author argues that a run of political changes has left Russia on the defensive across several regions. A student-led movement ousted Serbia's long-serving President Vucic in a late-October vote, removing a consistently pro-Russian voice in Europe. In Romania, a new pro-EU government ended a five-month deadlock after Bucharest shot down Russian drones over the Black Sea, and the author sees this as providing stability and likely firmer backing for Ukraine. Hungary's Orban, widely seen as Moscow's unofficial representative inside NATO and the EU, lost power in April, and his successor is described as more pragmatic toward Kyiv and firmer on Russia. The piece adds setbacks in Venezuela, Syria and the South Caucasus, while noting Russia's ties with China, Iran and North Korea remain strong and that it is too early to write off Putin.
brief.argument: Recent electoral and geopolitical setbacks in the Balkans, Central Europe and beyond are eroding Russia's influence, though Moscow retains significant partners and room to recover.

c5e12955725a1fc6.title: Last week’s brief Ukraine ceasefire did not stop Russian attacks on civilians
c5e12955725a1fc6.summary: A recent humanitarian ceasefire around the southern Ukrainian city of Oleshky made it possible to evacuate hundreds of residents, but Russian attacks on civilians elsewhere in Ukraine continue, writes Kristina Hook. The post Last week’s brief Ukraine ceasefire did not stop Russian attacks on civilians appeared first on Atlantic Council .

ai.sum: A brief humanitarian ceasefire around Oleshky allowed evacuation of civilians, but Russian attacks on civilians elsewhere in Ukraine continued.

brief.summary: The authors argue that the brief, localised Oleshky ceasefire, which allowed hundreds of civilians to leave Russian-occupied Oleshky, was a real humanitarian success but should not be read as a shift in Moscow's position. They say the evacuation must not obscure what made it necessary: Russian occupation, the 2023 Kakhovka dam destruction, and mining that emptied a city of about 24,000 people to under 2,000. They contend that staged cooperation, such as Ukrainian and Russian officials thanking each other, reflects Kyiv's wish to save lives rather than trust in the performance, and that the Russian ombudswoman involved is accused of facilitating child deportations. They note that Russian strikes on civilians continued during the pause, including a deadly attack on a school aid point in Zaporizhzhia the day after it ended. The authors call for scrutiny of humanitarian pauses and for continued independent monitoring and accountability.
brief.argument: The Oleshky ceasefire saved lives but does not signal any broader Russian willingness to stop attacking Ukrainian civilians or end the invasion.
recommendations: Keep independent monitoring and accountability in focus after humanitarian pauses end
Do not treat localised, staged cooperation as evidence of a change in Russian policy
Use precise language that attributes responsibility for civilian suffering to Russia

brief.summary: The authors, writing for Al Majalla, review Philippe Jaenada's Goncourt-winning novel The Unknown Woman of Quai de Javel, about an unsolved 1949 Paris murder. They argue the book's real interest lies less in the crime than in recovering the life of victim Louise Cansot, a Breton model in Montparnasse circles, and in the gap between documentary records and what imagination can reconstruct. The piece notes Jaenada's use of AI in research, which places the novel inside the year's authorship debate, and praises his reversal of the usual true-crime focus from killer to victim. It also flags a risk: the author's interventions and digressions sometimes crowd out the woman at the centre. Finally, it points to the concentration of all four shortlisted novels within one publishing group, Madrigall, as a structural issue for prize diversity.
brief.argument: Jaenada's novel matters most as an act of recovering a forgotten woman's life, using documentary inquiry while openly acknowledging the limits of knowledge and the writer's freedom to imagine.

b932152705f17e88.title: Can Washington and China Build Confidence Around AI and Stability?
b932152705f17e88.summary: In the lead-up to General Secretary Xi Jinping’s September 2026 visit to the White House to discuss, among other topics, AI, U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent met with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng at JPMorgan Chase’s New York City offices. At the meeting, U.S. officials proposed establishing a dialogue between the United States and China, which would serve as a mechanism for notification of AI-related national security incidents. Bessent clarified the intent as: “We…

ai.sum: Analysis proposes a US-China dialogue mechanism on AI and stability ahead of Xi Jinping's planned September 2026 White House visit, after Bessent met He Lifeng in New York.

brief.summary: The author argues that proposed US-China AI dialogues and communication channels are not arms control, since they lack enforcement or verification and leave AI innovation and power balance untouched. Instead they should be judged as confidence-building measures, drawing on Cold War precedents such as the hotline, Incidents at Sea Agreement and Nuclear Risk Reduction Centers. The piece sees real reasons for optimism, namely shared concern about AI's role in nuclear decisions, but notes that no AI-triggered crisis comparable to 1962 has occurred, that the two sides define key terms such as lethal autonomous weapons and human control differently, that AI is a general-purpose technology rather than a discrete weapon, and that private firms have interests that may diverge from governments'. The author says the first talks should focus narrowly on the 2024 agreement on human control over nuclear use, sharpen definitions, identify observable behavioural indicators, and avoid contentious issues such as export controls and AI governance. Domestic regulation of AI firms, such as incident reporting, is presented as supporting the credibility of bilateral measures.
brief.argument: US-China AI dialogues can reduce escalation risks only if they are scoped as confidence-building measures focused narrowly on nuclear-related AI risk, not as arms control.
recommendations: Keep the dialogue narrowly focused on human control over nuclear-use decisions and avoid broader disputes such as export controls and AI governance.
Use early rounds to sharpen shared definitions of autonomy and human control, including for early warning and nuclear command and control.
Identify observable behavioural indicators and escalation off-ramps rather than restricting AI development itself.
Build domestic regulatory mechanisms for AI firms, such as incident reporting, to lend credibility to bilateral measures.
